summary: Light at the southern tip of Haida Gwaii: a 1913 concrete tower on St. James Island, first shown in 1914, now a white mast; a wartime radar unit shared the island.

lens.note: As announced in the 1914 notice; current lens not in the sources read.

structures.note: White octagonal reinforced-concrete tower with a red metal lantern (notice as quoted by LighthouseFriends); demolished after deactivation (Rowlett).
White mast on the summit (LighthouseFriends, 2021; Coast Guard list 'White mast'); Rowlett describes a 4 m post on a square equipment shelter.

access.note: Reached only by boat or helicopter; site status unknown (Rowlett). LighthouseFriends says access is very hazardous and may be restricted.

events.note: Concrete tower completed in late 1913; apparatus and keeper installed after it.
Light announced for about 15 February 1914 in the Department's notice; Rowlett gives 1914 as the station's start.
The keeper's dwelling was lost to fire; a new dwelling was built and the keeper used the boathouse meanwhile.
On 7 December 1941 a wartime instruction put the light out, the first time since 1914.
Radar unit established on the island. LighthouseFriends gives 26 August 1943; the radar history gives 11 November 1943.
Radar unit closed on 10 August 1945 (both sources).
A member of the radar unit disappeared while fishing alone near the station on 27 April 1945; no trace was found (radar history).
Lantern removed when a new aerobeacon was installed.
LighthouseFriends dates automation to 1961, the year its keeper list ends. Disputed: see the 1992 entry.
Original octagonal concrete tower replaced by a metal tower (radar history); Rowlett says the original was demolished after deactivation.
Radar history: site automated, old buildings dismantled except the light mast. The station record also gives 1992. Disputed with 1961.
Flashing white light shown from a white mast on the summit of the island.

corrections.why: The 4.0 m figure in the record (from Wikidata) is the height of the present post. The 1913 concrete tower was 44 ft (about 13 m) tall, per LighthouseFriends' account of the 1914 notice.
The tower was completed in late 1913 (Department report for 1913-14); the light was announced for February 1914.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1914 is the first-light year. The tower was built in 1913 and the notice set the light for about 15 February 1914. Rowlett also gives 1914 as the station's establishment year. The 1984 date in the record belongs to the replacement tower.

The 1984 date in Rowlett and in the record is the replacement metal tower, not the first lighthouse. The 1913 concrete tower was octagonal and 13 m high (44 ft); the present structure is a white mast.

notes_for_editor:
Sources. LighthouseFriends (3) is a copyrighted community site: used for facts only, paraphrased, with one-line quotes. Its account of the 1914 notice to mariners is second-hand (the notice itself was not read), and the story says so. The radar-unit history (4) is a veterans' association page; its wartime detail is attributed to it. Rowlett (5) is a directory.

Disputed, not settled in the story: (a) automation: LighthouseFriends says 1961 (its keeper list ends with Bournazel, 1956-1961); the radar history and the station record say 1992. (b) Radar-unit start: 26 August 1943 (LighthouseFriends) against 11 November 1943 (radar history). (c) Range: the 1914 notice says 24 miles without saying nautical or statute; the Coast Guard list says 13 nm. (d) Rowlett's focal plane of 315 m (1033 ft) does not match the Coast Guard's 96 m; the 96 m figure is used.

Keepers. Taylor Ash's 1914 date is LighthouseFriends'. The 1913-14 Department report says the November 1913 party was to install apparatus and keeper, so the first keeper may have arrived in late 1913. The 1913-14 'Statement of lightstations and names of lightkeepers' for British Columbia (printed p. 71-72, scan pp. 78-79) lists names, appointment months and dates, but the OCR splits them into separate columns. I did not match any name to a date by column position, so no keeper date comes from that table. A checker should read the page image before relying on any date from it. The 1913 contract table (1914v48, scan 60, printed 53) has a 'St. James, Cape' row with a 40-foot tower, but its rows are also split, so I did not use it.

Name-only coincidence, not linked: a Stanley F. Lawrence is listed at Cape St. James 1921-1931 and a Stanley Fredrick Lawrence at Holland Rock 1920-1921. No source connects them, so no other_stations link is made.

No women keepers are named in the sources read. The lightkeeper's wife (1943-45, radar history) is not named.

Not reached: the Haida Gwaii Museum photo records (haidagwaii.emuseum.com) and Nauticapedia return 403, so their captions are not used. Chronicling America searches for Cape St. James found nothing relevant. LighthouseFriends says the southern third of the archipelago lies in Gwaii Haanas National Park Reserve; I did not check whether St. James Island is inside it, so the story does not say so.

Current lens and any fog signal are not in the sources read.
